slide.title: Why So Generic?
slide.body: Left: grey chat bubble with blurred lines labelled 'vague prompt'. Right: teal chat bubble with clear lines labelled 'clear prompt'. Small tag: Prompt Engineering Masterclass · Lesson 1.

scenes.voiceover: You type write an email to a client into an AI chat tool. In a few seconds, you get a polite, well-written email. But it could be sent by anyone, to anyone, about anything. Why did a clever tool give you such a general answer?

slide.title: How AI Chat Tools Respond to You

scenes.voiceover: Hi, and welcome to the Prompt Engineering Masterclass. In this first lesson, we look at how AI chat tools respond to you, and why your words matter so much.

scenes.stock_query: person typing message on laptop office
scenes.voiceover: An AI chat tool, such as Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini, is a program that reads the text you type and writes a reply. You do not need any technical knowledge. You type a request in normal language, which is called a prompt, and the tool responds.

slide.title: How a reply is made
slide.body: Your prompt + patterns from training → 'predict a likely answer, word by word' → reply. Greyed-out icons outside the box: inbox, files, client, team, goal, labelled 'not known unless you say'.

scenes.voiceover: The tool learned from a very large amount of text during its training. When you send a prompt, it predicts a likely, useful answer, word by word, based on your words and the patterns it learned. It does not look into your inbox or your files unless you give it that material. And it does not know your client, your team or your goal.

slide.title: Two surprises
slide.body: 1. Vague prompt → generic answer (gaps filled with safe choices). 2. Same prompt → different answers (predicting, not looking up). Fix for both: clear context and instructions = fewer gaps.

scenes.voiceover: This explains two surprises. First, a vague prompt gives a generic answer. The tool fills the gaps with safe, common choices. Second, the same prompt can give different answers, because the tool is predicting, not looking up one fixed answer. Clear context and instructions leave fewer gaps, so the answers vary less.

scenes.stock_query: new employee first day friendly office
scenes.on_screen_text: A capable colleague on day one
scenes.voiceover: Here is a simple way to picture it. Imagine a capable new colleague on their first day. They have read a lot and write well. But they know nothing about your team, your client or your goal.

slide.title: Briefing the new colleague
slide.body: Left: 'Write to the client.' → polite, general. Right: 'Write to Mr Diallo, delivery 3 days late, apologise, offer Friday.' → excellent, specific.

scenes.voiceover: If you say write to the client, they produce something polite and general. If you say write to Mr Diallo, whose delivery was three days late, apologise, and offer Friday, they can do excellent work. The AI tool is that new colleague, every time you start a new chat.

scenes.stock_query: account manager working at desk city
scenes.voiceover: Let's see this at work. Mariana is an account manager at an engineering firm in São Paulo. A client's inspection visit has to move, because a key engineer is ill.

slide.title: Before
slide.body: Prompt (code style): 'Write an email to a client.' → Output card: friendly email, 'thank you for your continued partnership'. Red notes: no visit, no date, no reason.

scenes.voiceover: Her first prompt is just five words: write an email to a client. The tool returns a friendly email about their continued partnership. Nothing in it is wrong, but she cannot send it. It does not mention the visit, the new date or the reason.

slide.title: After
slide.body: Write a short email to [CLIENT CONTACT], facilities manager at a food-processing company. Our site inspection planned for Tuesday must move because our lead engineer is ill. Offer Thursday or Friday morning instead. Apologise once, keep a professional and warm tone, and ask them to confirm by Monday.

scenes.voiceover: Her second prompt is a few lines. It says who the reader is, that the Tuesday inspection must move because the lead engineer is ill, and that she can offer Thursday or Friday morning. It asks for one apology, a warm, professional tone, and a reply by Monday.

slide.title: The difference
slide.body: Before: general, unusable. After: visit named, reason, two dates, reply by Monday (green ticks). One phrase changed, then sent.

scenes.voiceover: This time, the email names the visit, gives the reason in one sentence, offers both dates and asks for a reply by Monday. Mariana changes one phrase and sends it.

scenes.on_screen_text: No tricks. Just the right information.
scenes.voiceover: Notice that she used no special tricks. She gave the information a new colleague would need. She also used a placeholder instead of the client's real name. You will learn more about that in lesson three.

slide.title: Before you press regenerate
slide.body: "Did I tell it who, what and why?"

scenes.voiceover: A common mistake is to think a generic answer means the tool is not very smart, and to keep pressing regenerate. Usually, the problem is missing information. Before you judge the output, ask yourself: did I tell it who, what and why? Adding two or three lines of context often helps more than asking again with the same words.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. It predicts from your prompt and training; it doesn't know your situation. 2. Vague → generic; same prompt → different answers. 3. Clear context = fewer gaps, often better output.

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, an AI chat tool predicts a likely answer from your prompt and its training. It does not know your situation unless you tell it. Second, vague prompts get generic answers, and the same prompt can give different answers. Third, clear context and instructions leave fewer gaps, so the output is often more useful and more consistent.

scenes.on_screen_text: Next: The Anatomy of a Strong Prompt
scenes.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, you will ask Claude for an email to a client, first with five words, then with who, what and why. Then you compare the two answers in three short points. It takes about fifteen minutes. In the next lesson, we look at the anatomy of a strong prompt. See you there.
